title: Activation-aware quant scheduler field notes
content:
Quick field notes + experiment log for the activation-aware quantization scheduler prototype (aka token-precision shuffler). Purpose: measure latency/throughput gains and quality regressions when switching precision per-token or per-layer based on activation magnitude heuristics, and evaluate kernel switching cost with AWQ/GPTQ/INT8/FP8 kernels.

Background and motivation:
- We observed tail latency spikes on mixed workloads where some batches have many long-generation requests interleaved with short ones. Static quant profiles (global INT8 or FP8) either hurt quality for sensitive prefixes or leave cost on the table.
- Hypothesis: cheaply detect high-variance activation segments and route those tokens to higher-precision execution (FP8 or full FP16) while running the rest in lower precision (INT8/AWQ). Benefit target: reduce average token cost ~15–25% while keeping quality delta under a small threshold (e.g., <0.8% rouge/perp delta on eval set) and not increasing p95 latency more than 5%.

Experiment setup:
- Hardware: A100-80GB (node-a), H100-80GB (node-b) for cross-arch comparisons.
- Models: open-7b (baseline FP16), open-7b-quant variants: int8-awq, gptq-int8, fp8-e4m3-style prototype. All models compiled with the runtime's kernel selection enabled.
- Workloads: three synthetic traces derived from production logs: short-chat (mean output 40 tokens), long-context-assist (mean 480 tokens, many long-memory prefixes), mixed-burst (random mix of 5–800 tokens). Also a small human-eval prompt set (80 prompts) measuring generation quality (BLEU/ROUGE/perplexity and a manual read-through).
- Metrics captured: median latency, p95/p99 token latency, tokens/sec throughput, GPU utilization, GPU memory headroom, end-to-end RLHF-style quality proxies (perp delta on eval prompts), and a tokenwise divergence rate (percent of tokens that differ when comparing lower-precision output to FP16 reference at sampling seeds).

Activation-aware scheduler design (prototype):
- Lightweight activation-signal sampler at layer N (default N = mid layers 16–26 for the 7B model). We sample the L2 norm of activations for each token window (sliding window width 4 tokens) and compute a small exponential moving average.
- Threshold rules: if scaled activation > T_high -> mark token high-fidelity; between T_low and T_high -> medium-fidelity; below T_low -> low-fidelity.
- Mapping: low -> INT8 (AWQ kernel preferred), medium -> GPTQ variant or FP8, high -> FP16/FP8-high-precision lane. Kernel switch is executed at micro-batch boundaries when possible; for streaming tokens we tested an in-flight kernel swap with KV-cache alignment (expensive).
- Fallback: if kernel swap latency + expected high-token time > static FP16 expected time for remaining sequence, scheduler keeps current precision to avoid oscillation.

Key observations (numbers are median/approx across three runs unless noted):
- Throughput: mixed-burst saw overall tokens/sec increase of 18% on A100 when using activation-aware scheduler vs static FP16 baseline (from ~23k tok/s to ~27k tok/s). Gains concentrated on low-fidelity majority tokens (~70% of tokens flagged low).
- Latency median: median token latency improved ~12%.
- Tail latency: p95 increased ~4–6% in scenarios where kernel swaps were frequent (streaming long-context). When we constrained swaps to happen only on micro-batch boundaries p95 actually improved slightly vs baseline due to batching benefits.
- Kernel switch cost: warm-to-warm kernel switch (same kernel family but different code path) cost ~0.45–0.7 ms per swap on A100; cold-first-time switch with JIT ~2.1–3.6 ms. H100 numbers were ~30% lower for warm switches but JIT cold penalty similar.
- Quality (perp/rouge): on the human-eval set, activation-aware runs with mapping low=INT8, medium=FP8, high=FP16 produced mean perplexity delta +1.1% vs FP16 baseline; rouge drop ~0.7. These are within our target but note distribution: ~5% of prompts showed >3% quality degradation localized to named-entity spans.
- Token divergence: ~4.5% tokenwise divergence overall for the three-way mapping; for tokens marked low divergence was 6.1%, medium 2.8%, high 0.4%. Divergence correlated strongly with activation peaks (as expected).
- Memory & utilization: lower-precision lanes reduced average GPU memory by ~7–9% (more headroom for KV cache), enabling larger batch sizes and better amortization for short chats.

Failure modes and gotchas:
- Oscillation: tokens with activation near thresholds produce flip-flopping between precision decisions across sliding windows, causing repeated kernel switches and QoS blips. Mitigation: hysteresis window (stay-in-precision for at least N tokens) reduces oscillation but can hurt responsiveness. Tuned N=6 tokens was a reasonable tradeoff in our traces.
- Prefix sensitivity: model behavior occasionally changes dramatically if early prefix tokens are lowered in precision. For tasks with entity copying or exact-match constraints, fallback policy must default to higher precision for primary entity segments (we add a simple prefix whitelist heuristic triggered by token-level OOV/NER detector).
- Cold path cost: first-time kernel codegen/JIT dominates at tail of short sessions. Need pre-warm heuristics for kernels likely to be used for that customer's model combo.

Kernel interactions and selection notes:
- AWQ kernels are very efficient for low-fidelity paths; we observed best throughput on INT8-AWQ for long-dense-token sequences with small vocab tokens. AWQ also has less jitter in p95 than older gptq kernels in our runs.
- GPTQ-int8 variant gave slightly better tokenwise fidelity at cost of 7–9% lower throughput vs AWQ on A100.
- FP8 proposals (e4m3-like) live in middle ground: quality much closer to FP16 while still giving 10–12% throughput improvements over FP16 when kernels are optimized. Current FP8 kernels in runtime remain experimental and require additional register tiling to reach parity on H100.

Practical recommendations (short-term):
- Ship scheduler in opt-in beta behind a routing flag for specific customers with mixed workload profiles and non-critical exact-match SLAs. Document expected behavior and caveats.
- Default heuristic: low threshold to capture majority-of-tokens cases and only enable micro-batch boundary switches by default to avoid p95 regressions.
- Provide dashboard metrics: percent tokens in each fidelity bucket, kernel switch frequency, median switch cost, and tokenwise divergence heatmap by prefix position. Tie quality regression alerts to our existing eval harness (post-serve sampling).

Longer-term research & engineering items:
- Profile-guided threshold tuning: offline sweeps to map activation distribution to expected divergence and find Pareto optimal thresholds per model family. Automate with small calibration pass during model onboarding. (INF ticket referenced.)
- Kernel warm pool: pre-jit and maintain a per-node small hotset of kernel variants tuned for customer model fleets to avoid cold penalties. Explore memory tradeoffs of resident kernels vs spare headroom.
- NER-aware scheduling: integrate lightweight NER/heuristic that pins tokens corresponding to sensitive spans to high-fidelity lanes. Evaluate latency/quality tradeoffs.
- Adaptive hysteresis: learn hysteresis length per workload to balance oscillation and responsiveness. Could be simple RL or bandit.

Immediate TODOs for next run:
- Expand eval set to include more entity-heavy prompts from enterprise customers (ask CS for curated set).
- Run longer stability run (72h) on H100 cluster with production traffic replay to characterize long-tail JIT churn and kernel memory fragmentation.
- Implement per-node kernel warm-pool prototype (PR #912 references initial scripts).
- Add instrumentation to tracing to attribute end-to-end quality regressions to token-fidelity decision with trace IDs.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally rough — goal is to capture field learnings and concrete next steps. Looking for feedback on threshold heuristics and whether we should surface a per-customer SLA knob to disable low-fidelity path for a customer's top-k routes.
- Marcus: please paste relevant production traces (anonymized) into linked confluence page. Priya: can you run the 72h replay on H100 test cluster next week? Tomas: would love your kernel warm-pool sketch and microbench scripts.

End of notes.
